After decades of exposure to harsh desert condition s, high visitation, and limited access for routine maintenance—common challenges for remote facilities—the Echo Bay restroom has experienced functional decline and deteriorated building elements such as, plumbing fixtures, windows, doors, lighting, and roofing. Rehabilitating this restroom will allow the following benefits for the park: • Restore essential infrastructure supporting safe and sanitary visitor recreation. • Improve durability and lifespan in a remote, desert environment. • Enhance accessibility for all visitors, in compliance with federal requirements. • Reduce maintenance backlogs and prevent service disruptions. • Promote visitor comfort, safety, and resource protection. The 418‑square‑foot restroom at the remote Echo Bay picnic area was built to serve these visitors. Its construction reflected design priorit ies common to NPS facilities of that era: simple masonry structures, stainless‑steel fixtures , metal doors and windows, and clay tile roofs—materials chosen for durability, ease of clea ning, and resistance to vandalism. Over time, the facility became a dependable service poin t for families, boaters, anglers, and travelers using the broader Echo Bay recreation corridor. The restroom provides essential sanitation service s in an otherwise undeveloped area of the recreation site. Its primary functions include: • Supporting day‑use recreation, particularly picnick ing, shoreline access, and boat‑related activities. • Offering a safe, hygienic facility in a remote loca tion where alternative services are limited or distant. • Enabling the National Park Service to provide basic visitor amenities in accordance with public health standards and NPS operational policies. • Reducing resource impacts by centralizing waste man agement and sanitary access
